question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $(x - 1)^{2}y^{′} =-2$ that satisfies the condition $y(2) = 1$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
y'=- \frac{2}{(x - 1)^{2}}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y'\,\text{d}x & =\int (- \frac{2}{(x - 1)^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\ y & =(-2)\int (\frac{1}{(x - 1)^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\ & =(-2)(- \frac{1}{x - 1})+C \\ & =\frac{2}{x - 1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=\frac{2}{x - 1}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(2)=1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(\frac{2}{(2) - 1})+C \\ 1 & =2+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=-1 + \frac{2}{x - 1}.
$$

Find the particular solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=4 x^{2}+3 e^{- 2 x}+4 \cos{(x )}$ that satisfies the condition $f(0)=3.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The derivative is already isolated, so we have

$$
f'(x)=4 x^{2}+3 e^{- 2 x}+4 \cos{(x )}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4 x^{2}+3 e^{- 2 x}+4 \cos{(x )})\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =\int (4 x^{2})\,\text{d}x + \int (3 e^{- 2 x})\,\text{d}x + \int (4 \cos{(x )})\,\text{d}x \\ & =(4)(\frac{x^{3}}{3}) + (3)(- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}) + (4)(\sin{(x )})+C \\ & =\frac{4 x^{3}}{3}- \frac{3 e^{- 2 x}}{2}+4 \sin{(x )}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x)=\frac{4 x^{3}}{3}- \frac{3 e^{- 2 x}}{2}+4 \sin{(x )}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0)=3$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =(\frac{4 (0)^{3}}{3}) + (- \frac{3 e^{- 2 (0)}}{2}) + (4 \sin{((0) )})+C \\ 3 & =(0) + (- \frac{3}{2}) + (0)+C \\ C & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x)=\frac{4 x^{3}}{3} + 4 \sin{(x )} + \frac{9}{2} - \frac{3 e^{- 2 x}}{2}.
